title: Every other way in
goal: Besides sound: type a word as it looks, from a shorter word inside it, or as a one-stroke short form.

blocks.x: Every word is also held as its letters read, a syllable at a time, even where the dictionary hears something else.

head: Word
Outline
What it shows
rows: *con* with an o, *tem* with an e

items: Each vowel letter may be short (`A`), long (`AEU`) or weak (`U`).
*c*, *g* and *s* may be hard or soft.
A silent *e* is optional: at the end (*table*) and before a consonant (*move* + *ment*).

blocks.x: A shorter word, then the rest
If a word starts with a word that has its own one-stroke outline, strike that word, then spell the rest from one stroke up.

A word that sounds like a commoner one and has no joins of its own takes that word's path plus a star stroke: [[ok|O/+KAEU/+*]] follows *okay*; a name follows its sound-alike the same way ([[matt|PHAT/+*]]).
Most long words also have a one-stroke short form. The derivable one is the **skeleton**: keep the first consonants, the stressed vowel and every consonant after it; drop the rest.

Every word gets its skeleton. Other short forms (dropping an unstressed first syllable, shelling) cover only the commonest 8,000 words and are not guessable. Learn short forms for long words you type often; use joins for the rest.

items: Know a one-stroke form? Use it (Lookup if unsure).
A stem you know plus an ending? Join them (lesson 10).
A prefix or two words? Join those (lesson 11).
Otherwise sound it out, syllable by syllable (lesson 12).
Or spell it as it looks, if that is how you see the word.
